Mohammad Reza Pahlavi (26 October 1919, 27 July 1980) was the last Shah of Iran, reigning from 1941 to 1979 as the second monarch of the Pahlavi dynasty. He succeeded his father, Reza Shah, and ruled the Imperial State of Iran until his overthrow in the Islamic Revolution.
During his reign, he assumed the title Shahanshah (lit. 'King of Kings'), and held several other titles, including Aryamehr (lit. 'Light of the Aryans') and Bozorg Arteshtaran (lit.

Born in Tehran, Pahlavi was named crown prince upon his father's coronation in 1926, and later served as an officer in the Iranian Army. The Anglo-Soviet invasion of Iran in 1941 forced Reza Shah's abdication and Mohammad Reza's accession to the throne.

body.text: His early reign was marked by political instability, including the Iran crisis of 1946 and a turbulent struggle for power with prime minister Mohammad Mosaddegh, who nationalized the British-owned oil industry with widespread popular support. However, a subsequent decline in oil exports and mounting economic difficulties weakened Mosaddegh's position.

Amid efforts to preserve his premiership by expanding his authority, Mosaddegh was removed from office in the 1953 Iranian coup d'état, carried out by pro-monarchy forces with British and American involvement. The coup consolidated the Shah's power, paving the way for increasingly autocratic rule.

In 1963, the Shah introduced the White Revolution, a broad program of economic and social modernisation accompanied by heavy investment in infrastructure and domestic industry, aimed at realising his vision of a "Great Civilization". Iran subsequently experienced rapid economic growth, with real GDP per capita nearly tripling between 1963 and 1976.

Living standards improved substantially, although the economic benefits were unevenly distributed. With American support, the Shah undertook an extensive military buildup, establishing Iran as the preeminent military power in the Persian Gulf, and independently sought to extend the country's influence into the Indian Ocean.

The 1973 Sale and Purchase Agreement effectively nationalised Iran's petroleum operations, and surging oil revenues thereafter fuelled an expansion of government investment. However, rapid spending strained the country's absorptive capacity, contributing to inflation, shortages, and persistent economic inequality.

Discontent over Iran's socioeconomic conditions and political repression fuelled growing opposition to the monarchy in the late 1970s. In January 1978, a newspaper article attacking dissident cleric Ruhollah Khomeini sparked protests that rapidly developed into nationwide demonstrations.

The crisis intensified with the Cinema Rex fire, the Jaleh Square massacre, and widespread strikes beginning in October, leaving the Shah's position increasingly untenable. On 16 January 1979, the Shah left Iran for exile, transferring his duties to a regency council.

Within a month, however, the monarchy collapsed, and Khomeini emerged as the supreme leader of the new Islamic republic. After encountering difficulties obtaining asylum in various countries amid the Iran hostage crisis, Pahlavi died in exile on 27 July 1980 in Egypt, where he had been welcomed by President Anwar Sadat.

Pahlavi's legacy remains divisive, reflecting his authoritarian rule, political repression, human rights violations, and close alignment with Western powers, alongside his efforts to modernize Iran's economy and enhance its geopolitical influence.

Positive views of his reign have persisted among segments of the Iranian population and diaspora, becoming particularly visible during the 2025, 2026 Iranian protests through pro-Pahlavi and monarchist slogans.
Early life, family and education
Mohammad Reza was born on 26 October 1919 in Tehran to Reza Khan (later Reza Shah Pahlavi), a brigadier general in the Persian Cossack Brigade, and his second wife, Tadj ol-Molouk.

His father was the son of Major Abbas-Ali Khan, an army officer of Mazandarani origin, and Noush-Afarin Ayromlou, whose family had emigrated to Iran from either Georgia or Yerevan in the nineteenth century following the Russo-Persian Wars.
His mother was born in Baku, Russian Empire (present-day Azerbaijan), and was the daughter of Teymūr Khan Ayromlou, an Iranian army general of Ayrum descent.

Mohammad Reza was Reza Khan's eldest son and the third of his eleven children by four women. He was born alongside his twin sister, Ashraf, his other full siblings were his older sister, Shams, and younger brother, Ali Reza.

His father reportedly regarded the birth of his first son as a good omen and called him khosh-ghadam (lit. In November 1919, following the enactment of Iran's surname law, Reza Khan adopted the surname Pahlavi, derived from the historical designation for Middle Persian.
On 24 April 1926, the day before his father's coronation, six-year-old Mohammad Reza was proclaimed Crown Prince of the newly established Pahlavi dynasty.

" He also shared a close relationship with his mother, Tadj ol-Molouk, and his older sister Shams. Tadj ol-Molouk was assertive and deeply superstitious, encouraging her son's belief that he was destined for an important future.

Upon becoming Crown Prince, however, he was separated from his mother and sisters and was placed under the educational supervision of military officers. Reza Shah further ordered that everyone, including his mother and siblings, address the Crown Prince as "Your Highness" (vālā-hazrat).
Mohammad Reza had a difficult relationship with his father, whom he later described in his autobiography Mission for My Country as "one of the most frightening men" he had known.

Their relationship remained emotionally distant and highly formal, Reza Shah addressed his son using the formal shomā (شما) rather than the informal to (تو), both meaning "you", and expected the same formality in return.
Education

In 1931, at the recommendation of Minister of Court Abdolhossein Teymourtash, Reza Shah sent the Crown Prince to Institut Le Rosey, a private boarding school in Switzerland. He left Iran on 7 September 1931 and became the first Iranian heir apparent to be sent abroad for his education.

His adjustment to life in Switzerland was initially difficult. Accustomed to the deference afforded to him in Iran, he reportedly demanded that fellow students stand at attention in his presence, but soon adapted to the comparatively egalitarian environment of the school. As a student, Mohammad Reza played football for the school's team.

In addition to his native Persian, Mohammad Reza learned to speak English, French, and German fluently. He developed a lasting interest in French language and culture, writing for the school newspaper in French in 1935 and 1936, he credited Le Rosey with broadening his outlook and introducing him to Western culture.

He also befriended Ernest Perron, a teacher who introduced him to French literature and became one of his closest confidants. When Mohammad Reza returned to Iran in 1936, Perron accompanied him and subsequently remained associated with the royal court at the Marble Palace.

After returning to Iran, Mohammad Reza completed his secondary education and enrolled at the Madrasa Nezam, a military academy in Tehran. He graduated as a second lieutenant in 1938 and was subsequently promoted to captain, a rank he held until his accession to the throne.
From 1938 to 1941, he served as an army inspector, travelling throughout Iran to examine both civil and military installations.
Rise to power and rule as Shah
First marriage

One of the main initiatives of Iranian and Turkish foreign policy had been the Saadabad Pact of 1937, an alliance bringing together Turkey, Iran, Iraq, and Afghanistan, with the intent of creating a Muslim bloc that, it was hoped, would deter any aggressors.

President Mustafa Kemal Atatürk of Turkey suggested to his friend Reza Khan during the latter's visit that a marriage between the Iranian and Egyptian courts would be beneficial for the two countries and their dynasties, as it might lead to Egypt joining the Saadabad pact.

Dilawar Princess Fawzia of Egypt (5 November 1921, 2 July 2013) was daughter of King Fuad I of Egypt and Nazli Sabri, and sister of King Farouk I of Egypt. In line with Atatürk's suggestion, Mohammad Reza and the Egyptian Princess Fawzia were married on 15 March 1939 in the Abdeen Palace in Cairo.

Reza Shah did not participate in the ceremony. During his visit to Egypt, Mohammad Reza was greatly impressed with the grandeur of the Egyptian court as he visited the various palaces built by Isma'il "the Magnificent" Pasha, the famously free-spending khedive of Egypt, and resolved that Iran needed similarly grandiose palaces to match them.
